description.narrative: Private sector investment as well as the business environment in Africa are constricted by a low volume of funding and the high cost of borrowing. With the decline of Official Development Assistance (ODA) from 68% of financial inflows in 1900 to the continent to less than 25% by 2022, more African countries are turning to global capital markets to obtain financing for development. Over the next decade, African countries must finance critical investments, with annual estimates around $100 billion in infrastructure, $45 billion in energy, and $30 billion in climate change. Consequently, for Africa, the cost of this borrowing and the assurance of adequate financing are urgent development priorities.Ghana, Benin, Cote d’Ivoire and Kenya face significant challenges in obtaining favourable credit ratings due to perceived high lending risks. These suboptimal credit ratings hinder their access to affordable financing and investment. A new initiative by UNDP seeks to address these challenges, including inadequate technical skills and capacity to navigate the credit ratings process; limited access to relevant data and documentation necessary for accurate credit assessments; and capable resource persons in government ministries to liaise with rating agencies.The theory of change for this initiative is simple – if UNDP can contribute to narrowing the gap between African countries’ actual lending risk and the perceived risk reflected by the global credit ratings, the sovereign credit ratings of African countries will improve, debt service burdens will decrease, fiscal space will expand, and FDI inflows will increase. These enhancements will go a long way to resolving Africa’s development financing conundrum, helping accelerate its economic transformation and improve its business environment.
